facts.text: The Chinese name jiannian means cut and paste.
Jiannian is a decoration found mostly on temple roofs, ridges, and eaves.
Common jiannian subjects include dragons, phoenixes, birds, flowers, animals, and characters from folk stories.
On the roofs of Longshan Temple in Taipei, dragons and phoenixes are covered with pieces of glass and ceramics in many colors.
To make a jiannian figure, a craftsman first bends stainless steel wire into a frame, or skeleton, for the figure.
The wire frame is then covered with a sticky paste made of sticky (glutinous) rice and lime, which gives the figure its body.
Last, ceramic bowls are broken or cut into small pieces, shaped, and pressed into the paste on the surface of the figure.
Well-made pieces that use the rice-and-lime paste can keep their bright colors for more than 30 years, while cheaper methods fall apart much sooner.
Jiannian began in Chaozhou, in China's Guangdong Province, around 1600, during the Ming dynasty.
Chaozhou was a major center for making ceramics, so there was plenty of broken pottery for craftsmen to use.
Immigrants later brought jiannian to Taiwan, where it developed its own local style with Taoist themes and wishes for good luck.
The work is physically hard: craftsmen spend long hours on rooftops in summer heat and winter cold, and smashing pottery can cut their hands.
Learning jiannian takes years of patient practice, and few people are now drawn to the craft.
A survey in 2004 found 37 registered jiannian craftsmen.
Jiannian pieces look impressive from a few meters away, though they can look rough up close.
Because traditional craftsmen are growing old, passing on their skills has become a major challenge in Taiwan.
In September 2026, a training base opened in Pingtung City to teach new workers traditional skills, including jiannian, that are needed to repair old historic buildings.
